evidence_notes: Claim: the Face on Mars is a natural landform, not alien evidence. Support from source: landforms are common around Cydonia; Michael Malin's 1998 Mars Global Surveyor / Mars Orbiter Camera images showed a natural landform; the feature resembles a butte/mesa like Middle Butte, Snake River Plain, Idaho (a lava dome of similar height). A concession paragraph raises haze hiding alien markings and answers it with camera accuracy. ORG 4 (controlling idea stated early and held, opening and closing present, all body parts relate; but the three supports - Cydonia commonality, clearer image, Earth-landform analogy - could swap freely, so rung 5 fails). DEV 4 (connection stated for some support - 'These landforms being equal, show that it's normal...' - but rung 5 fails because the Cydonia-commonality support is a general gesture, not specific, and most explanations restate the evidence). CONV 3 (errors accumulate and the reader re-reads to repair: 'However, when Mars Global surveyor in April 5, 1998, Michael Malin was able to snap pictures' lacks a verb, and 'Although it may have unusual shadows, NASA could only wish that there would be possible evidence' is garbled; rung 4 fails). ARG 4 (rung 4 met - 'It being common, creates a slimmer chance of it being crafted by other life forms' states a why; rung 5 fails because although a counterargument is acknowledged and answered, the conclusion is exactly what the prompt's framing implies).

Claim: the Electoral College should be abolished (letter to a state senator). Reasons: voters hand their votes to electors rather than choosing the president directly; electors may break the trust placed in them. No named election, figure, or case anywhere. ORG 4 (controlling idea stated early and held, salutation/opening and a call-to-action closing present, both body parts relate; rung 5 fails because stripped of the 'this brings me to my next point' signposting the two body parts are near-redundant complaints that could swap). DEV 2 (rung 3 fails - no named case, no figure, no realized example; support is general throughout ('there is always that tiny percentage'), and 'they are setting themselves up for disaster' restates rather than explains). CONV 3 (errors accumulate - 'dis like', 'ballet' for ballot, missing spaces, comma splices; the long sentence about giving votes 'to some one else... not for the elector that that person actually put down on the ballet' has to be re-read and repaired, so rung 4 fails, but meaning stays recoverable so rung 3 holds). ARG 4 (rung 4 met - the essay says why the system is bad, tracing votes to electors who need not follow them; rung 5's 'at least one of' is satisfied by the concession 'It is true that the slate of electors is trusted... but there is always that tiny percentage', yet rung 5 fails because the conclusion, abolish it, is precisely what the prompt's framing implies).

Claim: driverless cars are not really driverless and are dangerous. Reasons: the cars still need the driver's attention (supported by a direct quotation from the source about cars notifying the driver in work zones and around accidents); they may not start or may be costly to repair; they could increase child deaths. ORG 4 (controlling idea plus roadmap in the opening, frame present, all three body parts relate; rung 5 fails - the three supports are independent and interchangeable). DEV 4 (rung 3 met by the quoted source passage; rung 4 met - 'If these cars were really driverless, they wouldn't need a driver to help them navigate' states the connection; rung 5 fails because paragraphs 3 and 4 are general speculation with no specific support and the death claim is unsupported). CONV 3 (errors accumulate - 'stiil', 'theroad', 'woul', comma splices - and 'Either way, these cars not start' plus 'The driverless cars, aren't even close to driving themselves, they still need...' require re-reading to repair, so rung 4 fails; meaning never has to be guessed). ARG 4 (rung 4 met by the definitional argument about what 'driverless' means; rung 5 fails - no opposing position is answered, 'no matter how safe they say it should be' dismisses rather than answers, and the anti position is what the prompt's framing implies).

Claim: keep the Electoral College because it keeps out problems and is fair. Support is two marked quotations (538 electors / 270 needed; the college avoids elections where no candidate receives a majority), plus two closing sentences lifted near-verbatim from the source on disputes being less likely and on voters expressing a political preference. ORG 3 (rung 4 fails - there is no closing at all; the essay stops mid-thought on the voter-preference sentence, so the frame is incomplete, and the final sentence does not clearly bear on the claim). DEV 3 (rung 3 met by the 538/270 figures; the trailing source phrasing is patchwritten - borrowed wording lightly stitched with no quotation marks and slight garbling - which caps this trait at 3; it is not predominantly copied, so not 1). CONV 2 (rung 3 fails - the opening 'I'm in favor of kipping the Electoral college that to the fact that keep out problems and its fare to evry one' has to be guessed at rather than repaired; 'tre', 'nether one', 'populat', 'eather' compound it and meaning is somewhat obscured). ARG 3 (rung 4 fails - the one 'because' clause, 'without the electoral college it will have a lot of candidates that they will not get a majority of vote', simply re-says the quotation it follows, and 'that shows that the popular vote is the one who wins' is a bare and invalid assertion; the position is clear and committed, so rung 3 holds).

Claim: not against driverless cars, because they can be safe, prevent texting-and-driving accidents, and alert you to take control. Support is realized hypotheticals: a mother feeding a crying baby while the car drives; a driver distracted by music; a teen answering a text; plus a loose reference to the passage on traffic jams and accidents. ORG 4 (controlling idea with roadmap stated early and held, frame present, all parts relate; rung 5 fails - the body reorders the intro's own list, showing the three supports are interchangeable). DEV 4 (rung 3 met by the realized mother-and-baby scenario; rung 4 met - 'A driverless car can prevent that becuase it can be driving itself and you could answer a call or a text'; rung 5 fails because most support is generic hypothesis ('maybe you can't find your phone') and explanations restate). CONV 3 (errors accumulate - 'gretest', 'becuase', 'their can be', 'rinigng' - and 'Not only because they drive themselves mean that they are amazing' and 'That would be if there isn't something else out there that will have to make you take control' need re-reading to repair, so rung 4 fails). ARG 4 (rung 4 met - the essay says why the car prevents texting accidents; rung 5 fails - the hedges are gestures rather than a real qualification, no opposing position is answered, and the pro conclusion is what the prompt's framing implies).

Claim: facial-expression-reading technology is not valuable in a classroom. Reasons: it provides no classroom benefit and education need not be amusing; looks are deceiving, illustrated by a realized case of a student momentarily confused by the clock whose confusion is reported to the instructor as topic confusion, causing an unnecessary interruption. A counterargument is quoted from paragraph 6 and answered. ORG 4 (controlling idea stated early and held, frame present, all parts relate; the rebuttal must come last, but the two supporting body parts could swap, so rung 5 fails). DEV 4 (rung 3 met by the realized misread-confusion case and the quotation; rung 4 met - 'Computers can't detect every emotion, and they surely can't detect where the cause of that emotion is coming from' does interpretive work; rung 5 fails because the 'no benefits' paragraph is rhetorical questions with no support at all). CONV 4 (rung 4 met - the many misspellings ('techonlogy', 'decieving', 'unnessisary', 'davantage') are visible but nothing has to be repaired on one pass; rung 5 fails because the errors are not merely occasional). ARG 5 (rung 5 met on both halves - the strongest available objection from the source is quoted and answered ('if a student is becoming confused then they should ask questions'), and the essay reaches beyond the prompt's binary to an explicit claim about what learning is for: 'Education doesn't have to be amusing or easy' and 'Boredom is commom in school, but that should not impact the ability to learn'; rung 6 fails because the answer redirects responsibility rather than showing the objection invalid or outweighed, and the question is not reframed).

Claim: Venus is a worthy pursuit despite the danger, for three reasons - it was once the most Earth-like planet, it was once covered by oceans, and scientists want to know why no spacecraft survives there. Each body paragraph quotes and cites the source (paragraph 4 sentences 2 and 3; passage 2 sentence 6) and adds detail (97 percent carbon dioxide, silicon carbide electronics lasting three weeks). ORG 4 (controlling idea stated early and held, opening and closing both present with every body part relating; rung 5 fails - the three reasons are listed in intro order and are wholly interchangeable, and the conclusion repeats the introduction almost word for word). DEV 4 (rung 3 met by the cited quotations and figures; rung 4 met because the connection is stated after each quote, but only as 'This means that...' restatement, which is exactly what caps this at 4 - rung 5 fails since the explanations add nothing the quotation did not already say). CONV 3 (errors accumulate - 'pursit', 'venuse', 'sciantists', 'fasinated', 'compareit' - and 'Scientists want to study venuse even though it dangers to see why its not like it use to be' has to be re-read and repaired; sentence shapes are also formulaic, one pattern per paragraph). ARG 3 (rung 4 fails - the essay never reasons about worthiness-despite-danger, only reports what scientists want ('This means that they are really into the thing that Venus was once like Earth'); the position is clear but the essay circles it, closing with a verbatim restatement of the opening and even attributing the position to 'people').

Claim: driverless cars will make daily life easier - saving money, reducing teen deaths, and driving for you when tired. Support drawn from the source: cars driven more than a million miles without a crash (paragraph 2); 'would use half the fuel of today's taxis'; the paragraph 7 quotation on cars notifying the driver, plus GM's vibrating driver's seat. ORG 4 (controlling idea with roadmap stated early and held, frame present, all body parts relate; rung 5 fails - the three supports appear in a different order in the body than in the intro and are freely interchangeable). DEV 4 (rung 3 met by the quoted figures and the vibrating-seat detail; rung 4 met - 'which mean that teens and young adult can let the car drive for a couple hours and text which can save their life'; rung 5 fails because the fuel paragraph is general speculation about who travels and why, and 'In American, almost most of the death of teenager are caused by texting while driving' is an unsupported generality). CONV 3 (errors accumulate heavily - 'reduced' for reduce throughout, 'elert' repeatedly, 'secceeded', 'functiong', misused 'whereas' - and 'In case of emergency whereas the car are not capable of functiong need the driver to take over' has to be re-read and repaired, so rung 4 fails; meaning stays recoverable so rung 3 holds). ARG 4 (rung 4 met by a genuinely reasoned chain - teens die texting, awareness campaigns fail because of peer and technology pressure, so letting the car drive saves lives; rung 5 fails because the alert-system passage describes a feature rather than answering an opposing position, and the pro conclusion is what the prompt's framing implies. Length was disregarded: this is the longest essay in the set but has the same three restated supports as the others.)

Claim: FACS emotion-reading devices are valuable and should be in classrooms. The one on-claim support is the boredom argument (teachers deliver lessons while students stop paying attention) plus the quoted Dr. Huang prediction that a classroom computer could recognize confusion or boredom and modify the lesson. The bulk of the middle - universality of expressions, the 3-D facial model, muscle detection, Ekman's six basic emotions - is exposition that does not bear on classroom value and is discarded before climbing. ORG 3 (rung 4 fails - the single body unit starts on classroom boredom, swerves into school affordability, then into how the technology works and Ekman's taxonomy; at least one part does not relate to the controlling idea and unity breaks). DEV 3 (rung 3 met by the cited Huang quotation, but rung 4 fails - after discarding the irrelevant exposition, what remains is listed rather than explained; the quotation is left unclosed and unexplained, and the reader supplies the connection between it and the position). CONV 2 (rung 3 fails - 'Its full name is glory is' and 'not all schools cant afford new high tech computers' force the reader to guess rather than repair; run-on sentences, 'studenr. Hat is becoming cinfused', 'instructure', 'mechine' and heavy exclamation compound it, and meaning is somewhat obscured). ARG 4 (rung 4 met - the essay states a why: students get bored and stop paying attention, the device would detect that, so teachers could correct the lesson; rung 5 fails - no opposing position is answered, the affordability point undercuts the claim and is dropped rather than engaged, and the conclusion is what the prompt's framing implies).

Claim: Venus should be studied despite the risk, derived from an explicit general principle - the universe is full of dangers and we do not abandon discovery because of them, so Venus is no different. Support: Venus was once Earth-like and still shows valleys, mountains and craters; it is our nearest option for a planetary visit; and the danger is being mitigated by hovering craft that gather intel without big risk and by electronics tested for Venus's climate. ORG 5 (rung 5 met - the two body parts cannot swap: the mitigation paragraph presupposes the value paragraph's case for wanting to go at all; rung 6 fails because the 'nearest option' reason sits outside the stated Earth-Venus-connection idea, the value paragraph does two jobs, and the closing merely repeats the opening's question rather than landing the argument somewhere new). DEV 4 (rung 3 met by concrete particulars - valleys, mountains, craters, hovering, heat-tested electronics; rung 4 met - 'to gather intel without a real big risk' and 'One day we might need that information' state connections; rung 5 fails because 'That should be more than enough reason' is assertion rather than explanation and the Earth-resemblance is never taken further into what the connection would teach). CONV 4 (rung 4 met - 'Astonomers', 'resmbles', 'wiith', 'plantery' and the missing subject in 'even though is will be difficult' are visible but the meaning arrives on one pass; rung 5 fails because the errors are more than occasional and control slips at the comma splice 'No, of course not, Then why should Venus be any different'). ARG 5 (rung 5 met on both halves - the governing principle is made explicit rather than implied, the danger objection is acknowledged and answered with the safer-methods paragraph, and the conclusion generalizes past the prompt's Venus-specific framing to whether difficulty should ever stop discovery; rung 6 fails because the strongest objection is answered only by reporting that scientists are working on it, not by showing it invalid or outweighed, and the reframe stays a one-sentence rhetorical gambit rather than a developed change of terms. Shortness was not held against it.)
